traveler: Emir Emin Arslan (al-Amir Amin Majid Arslan)
title: Choueifat to Buenos Aires: Emir, Exile, Consul, Citizen
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Choueifat, Mount Lebanon: birth into the house of Arslan
stops.campa: In the Druze hill town of ash-Shuwayfat, above the Beirut littoral, a son is born to the emira Zahiyya Shihab and the emir Majid Arslan: Amin, of a lineage the family traces past the Ma'nids to the old Lakhmid kings, and that has carried the title of emir in the Gharb of Mount Lebanon for centuries. His cousins hold the same rank across the mountain; among them, in the same village, a younger kinsman named Shakib Arslan will grow to be called Amir al-Bayan, Prince of Eloquence. Amin's own eloquence will be spent, in the end, four languages and three continents away.
suggested_refs: The Arslan family seat at Choueifat, seat of the Druze emirs of the Gharb since Ottoman times

stops.name: Beirut, the Jesuit college and the Madrasat al-Hikma
stops.campa: The emir's son is sent down from the mountain to Beirut, city of missions and printing presses, and takes his letters first at the Yasu'iyya, the Jesuit fathers' school, then at the Madrasat al-Hikma, founded by the Maronite bishop and historian Yusuf ad-Dabs. French he acquires early in these houses; Turkish a private tutor brings him at home. Here a Druze boy sits under a bifrontal education, Oriental and European at once, Arabic grammar beside French rhetoric, that will mark every page he writes. He finishes in 1891, and his father rewards him with a journey: Baalbek, Damascus, Nazareth, Bethlehem, Jerusalem, home by Carmel, Tyre and Sidon.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit Yasu'iyya and the Madrasat al-Hikma of Bishop Yusuf ad-Dabs, Beirut, of the 1880s
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

stops.name: Beirut, initiation into a Masonic lodge
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of August the young emir is received into a lodge of the Grand Orient de France in Lebanon, one more thread in the web of reformist Ottoman subjects, Muslim, Christian, Druze, Jewish, who use the lodges as cover and school for constitutionalist politics under a sultan who has suspended the constitution and jailed its friends. Freemasonry gives Amin Arslan a language of brotherhood across confession that his own mountain, parceled by sect, does not offer, and a network of correspondents that will serve him within four years, when the mudirate collapses and Beirut is no longer safe for him to remain in.
suggested_refs: Lodge of the Grand Orient de France in Lebanon, Beirut, 24 August 1889

stops.name: Nahiyat al-Gharb al-Aqsa, mudir of the Outer Gharb
stops.campa: Naum Pasha of Aleppo takes office as mutasarrif of Mount Lebanon, the autonomous province carved out after the massacres of 1860, and names Amin Arslan, twenty-four and just out of school, mudir of the Nahiya of the Farthest West, the hill country around his own Choueifat. He governs peasant villages where the old feudal dues still bind muqata'ji families like his own to the fellahin who work their land, and where every appointment is watched by six religious communities and by the Powers guaranteeing the charter. He administers with a reformer's hand, sympathetic already to the constitutionalists in exile, and so already sideways to the governor who appointed him.
suggested_refs: The mudirate seat of the Outer Gharb district under the Mutasarrifate of Mount Lebanon

stops.name: Choueifat, a life of Napoleon in Arabic
stops.campa: In number 1376 of the Beirut review Lisan al-Hal, dated the twenty-first of January, the first instalment appears of Tarikh Nabulyun al-Awwal, a life of Napoleon I in Arabic: the Corsican artillery lieutenant who made himself an emperor, served in weekly parts to a mountain province where rank is inherited and nothing is made. It is an odd first subject and a revealing one. Arslan is twenty-three, about to take an office his blood gave him, and has chosen the man who proved a career could be seized outright. Within eighteen months he will resign that office and spend fifty years proving the same thing with a pen.
suggested_refs: Tarikh Nabulyun al-Awwal, serialized in Lisan al-Hal, Beirut, from no. 1376, 21 January 1892
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015), citing Ghalib (1988): 101

stops.name: Baabda, the break with Naoum Pasha and the resignation
stops.campa: At Baabda, seat of the mutasarrif, the young mudir collides with Naum Pasha, the Ottoman-appointed governor of the mountain, over the running of his district and, behind it, over the whole question of reform. Arslan resigns rather than bend, a gesture the province reads correctly as constitutionalist defiance dressed as an administrative quarrel. It costs him the only office his family's rank had reliably guaranteed him. Within months he takes ship with his friend Salim Sarkis, a fellow Beiruti journalist, breaks the voyage briefly in Egypt, and comes on to Paris, carrying nothing of his emirate but its name and beginning, at twenty-five, the life of an exile.
suggested_refs: The residence of the mutasarrif Naoum Pasha at Baabda, seat of the Mount Lebanon government

stops.name: Paris, arrival among the Young Turk exiles
stops.campa: Arslan and Salim Sarkis land in a Paris crowded with Ottoman dissidents who print in a dozen languages what Constantinople forbids. With Sarkis and other Arabs he founds the Comité Turco-Syrien, and makes contact with the Lebanese reformer Khalil Ghanim and the Istanbuli Ahmed Riza. At a table in the café du Cardinal, on the boulevard, the three agree to found two papers, one Turkish and one Arabic, for the reopening of Parliament and the constitution of 1876. Arslan goes to the Bibliothèque Nationale to dig out the old Young Turk programme and announce its resurrection to the world; the party's only members are the three men at that table.
suggested_refs: The Comité Syrien-Turc of Paris exile journalism, 1890s

stops.name: Paris, Kashf an-Niqab lifts the veil
stops.campa: On the ninth of August the first number of Kashf an-Niqab, the Lifting of the Veil, appears, founded by Arslan with Salim Sarkis: an Arabic sheet printed beyond the Sultan's censors, smuggled back inside the empire's borders, that says in Paris what no press in Beirut or Damascus dares say of Abdülhamid's rule. It runs until the twenty-fifth of July of the following year. It is his first taste of a trade he will practice, on and off, for the rest of his life: the exile's newspaper as the only sovereignty left to a man whose province has disowned him, and the Yildiz Palace reads every number.
stops.quote: El sultán se desesperaba al ver en los grandes diarios de Europa noticias sobre la situación de Turquía, provenientes de los jóvenes turcos, y como tenía una prensa a sueldo que le costaba muy cara, pensó que debía de haber alguna potencia o algún rico partidario que nos subvencionaba.
stops.quote_source: Emín Arslán, Recuerdos de Oriente (Buenos Aires, 1918), p. 204
suggested_refs: Kashf an-Niqab, Paris, 9 August 1894 - 25 July 1895

stops.name: Paris, Turkiya al-Fatat, the bilingual review
stops.campa: Where Kashf an-Niqab spoke only Arabic, Turkiya al-Fatat, La Jeune Turquie, speaks French as well, a fortnightly directed by Khalil Ghanim with Arslan as secretary of the redaction, aimed now at the European chancelleries and salons whose opinion the exiles hope to bend. Its masthead calls it plainly a journal of political propaganda. Most articles go unsigned; the direction is credited to Order and Progress, the redaction to Love of Country. One piece Arslan does sign, on the fifth of June 1896: Le Parlement Français Insulté, on Constantinople boasting that it has bought French deputies with banquets.
suggested_refs: Turkiya al-Fatat / La Jeune Turquie, Paris, Dec. 1895 - mid-1897, directed by Khalil Ghanim

stops.name: Paris, La Revue Blanche and the Armenians of Constantinople
stops.campa: After Armenian revolutionaries seize the Ottoman Bank in Constantinople and reprisal answers with days of massacre in the streets, Arslan carries the story past the Arabic exile press into the French literary avant-garde itself. Four pieces of his run in La Revue Blanche across 1896, the review of the Natanson brothers and Mallarmé's circle: Les Affaires de Crète, Les Affaires d'Orient, Les Troubles de Syrie, and last Les Arméniens à Constantinople, in which he prints a Dashnaktsutiun communiqué entire and reproaches those Frenchmen who condemn the seizure while claiming descent from the men who took the Bastille. He ends by naming exactly which death he is waiting for.
stops.quote: Nous autres Ottomans nous ne voulons pas la mort de notre empire, mais nous attendons la mort de son sultan, cause de son malheur et des nôtres.
stops.quote_source: Emin Arslan, 'Les Arméniens à Constantinople', La Revue Blanche, Paris, 1896
suggested_refs: La Revue Blanche, vols. X-XI, Paris 1896, 'Les Arméniens à Constantinople'
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

stops.name: Paris, the truce with the Sultan and the road to Bordeaux
stops.campa: Four years of exile end, oddly, in an accommodation. The Sultan sends into Europe Ahmed Cemaleddin, a Circassian of his completest confidence, with a three-point pact. Arslan resists first: he has two brothers in prison, one sentenced to ten years for the crime of being found with a letter of his, the other to two for a copy of the paper. He fears a trap, and proposes six months' silence to test the Sultan's word. Cemaleddin will not have it. Arslan accepts at last on one condition, that the post keep him beyond the reach of the hand that grants it.
stops.quote: Vino a proponernos el pacto siguiente: 1.º El sultán daría una amnistía general; 2.º Nos reintegraría en nuestros puestos respectivos; 3.º Concedería la Constitución; y todo esto a una sola condición: que cesáramos en nuestra campaña y entráramos tranquilamente en nuestras casas.
stops.quote_source: Emín Arslán, Recuerdos de Oriente (Buenos Aires, 1918), pp. 211-212
suggested_refs: The 1897 truce negotiated by Ahmed Cemaleddin between the Sultan and the Young Turk exile press
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181
M. Ş. Hanioğlu, The Young Turks in Opposition (1995)

segments.name: Consul of a Sultan He Opposes (1897-1908)

stops.name: Bordeaux, first post under the Ottoman seal
stops.campa: Arslan takes up the consulate at Bordeaux, port of the Gironde, his first salary and his first office in a decade of politics without one. He is a strange sort of Ottoman official: a constitutionalist who has just been amnestied for anti-government journalism, appointed to represent the government he attacked, on the government's own bet that a fed dissident is a quieter one. He does the consul's ordinary business, shipping papers, the affairs of Ottoman subjects passing through the Atlantic port, while keeping, underneath, every conviction he carried out of Beirut four years before.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman consulate general at Bordeaux, 1897

stops.name: Brussels, eleven years as consul general
stops.campa: Within months Arslan is transferred to Brussels, where he will hold the consulate general for eleven years, longer than any other post of his life. Belgium under Leopold II is neutral, orderly, and full of the same émigré Ottoman politics he left in Paris. The Porte's own files, Hanioğlu found, record him appointed despite publishing activity the authorities frankly called hostile: they had failed to buy him home, so they gave him a desk instead. Arslan keeps a foot in both worlds, and no sultan's spies ever quite catch him at it cleanly enough to have him recalled.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman consulate general at Brussels, 1897-1908

stops.name: Brussels, the sealing of Damad Mahmud Pasha's house
stops.campa: Damad Mahmud Celaleddin Pasha, the Sultan's own brother-in-law turned Young Turk exile, lies dying near the Bois de la Cambre, and Ottoman intelligence knows it. Arslan is ordered to seal the house the moment he dies and seize the conspirators' papers; a watch is set to help him. Arslan contrives not to be notified of the death for fifteen hours, time enough for the Young Turks to empty the desk. One compromising valise they cannot reach; the French journalist Victor Taunay warns him, and Arslan arranges for that to vanish too. The story surfaces only in August 1908, in Le Temps and the Levant Herald.
suggested_refs: The Brussels residence and papers of Damad Mahmud Celaleddin Pasha, d. 17 January 1903
'Histoire des papiers de Mahmoud Pacha', Gil Blas and Le Temps, Paris, 27 August 1908
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181
Le Temps, Paris, 20 January 1903, p. 2 (the inventory)

stops.name: Brussels, resignation to join the Young Turk Revolution
stops.campa: News reaches Brussels that on the twenty-fourth of July the Committee of Union and Progress has forced Abdülhamid II to restore the constitution of 1876 and call elections for December, without a shot fired in the capital. In August Arslan resigns the consulate he has held for eleven years, the position that was itself the price of his 1897 truce, to go and take part in the revolution he spent fifteen years agitating for from exile. It is the one clean moment of his political life: constitutionalist theory and Ottoman office align, briefly, before the Committee's own turn toward centralism estranges him again.
suggested_refs: The 1908 Young Turk Revolution and the restoration of the Ottoman constitution

stops.name: Istanbul, the capital of the restored constitution
stops.campa: In October Arslan reaches the Ottoman capital, one of the last of the exiles to come in, and sees it for the first time in his life: forty years an Ottoman subject, twenty-five a mountain emir, fifteen a Paris and Brussels agitator, and never once the city he had been arguing about. He finds the country, he will write, in ruins, and the victors overconfident, astonished at their own bloodless success and blind to the Sultan's record and to the men their purges have thrown out of work. December's elections will send his cousin Muhammad Mustafa Arslan to the chamber as deputy for Latakia. It will not hold.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman Parliament reconvened at Istanbul after the 1908 revolution
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015), citing Arslán, Recuerdos de Oriente (1918): 103-104

stops.name: Istanbul, the countercoup and the cousin killed outside Parliament
stops.campa: The Thirty-First of March rising by the old calendar has soldiers and theology students in the streets, and Arslan is still in the capital when it takes its victims around the Parliament building. On the fifteenth of April his cousin Muhammad Mustafa Arslan, deputy for Latakia, is shot down in front of the chamber, killed in mistake for Hüseyin Cahid of the Tanin. The error compounds: the only Emir Arslan the European press knows is Emin, so Paris reports his death that same day, his friend Jules Claretie writes his obituary in Le Temps, and Brussels buries him in Le Vingtième Siècle.
stops.quote: Emir Arslan, député de Latakied, pris par mégarde pour Houssein Djahid, rédacteur au Tanine, a été tué devant le Parlement.
suggested_refs: Gil Blas, Paris, 15 April 1909, p. 2, the erroneous notice of Arslan's death
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

stops.name: Paris, consul general once more, under his old superior
stops.campa: Le Temps reports on the sixteenth of September that the Paris consulate is raised to a consulate general and that its new holder is the former consul at Brussels, the emir Emin Arslan. Why the post proves unwelcome is not certainly known; the likeliest reading, and the one his biographers favour, is the ambassador. Naum Pasha, the same mutasarrif of Mount Lebanon to whom he had handed his resignation before going into exile in 1893, now sits above him again. Arslan asks for a transfer, and hears in Paris that Rome has just seen the signing of a first consular protocol with a republic across the ocean.
suggested_refs: Le Temps, Paris, 16 September 1909, p. 3, the notice of Arslan's appointment
The Argentine-Ottoman consular protocol signed at Rome, 11 June 1910
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

segments.name: Buenos Aires, Consul of the Sultan (1910-1914)

stops.name: Puerto Madero, the Chili docks to a crowd of four thousand
stops.campa: The Messageries Maritimes steamer Chili, out of Bordeaux, boarded by Arslan at Lisbon in the week the Portuguese monarchy fell, puts in at Buenos Aires on the twenty-ninth of October. What waits on the mole is not the usual nothing that greets a consul. Columns have marched from the Sociedad Joven Otomana hall and from La Boca with banners; the crowd has stood more than three hours; when the Ottoman flag comes up the mast the bands play the Argentine anthem, the Ottoman, and the Marseillaise. He thanks them, and is driven to the Plaza, several blocks of people walking behind the cars.
suggested_refs: The steamship Chili, Messageries Maritimes, arriving Buenos Aires 29 October 1910
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015), citing Hyland (2011): 565

stops.name: Buenos Aires, first Spanish, first press, first thanks to González
stops.campa: Arslan lands with no Spanish and leans on Wadi Schamun, editor of the Arabic paper Assalam, to find his footing. On the fifth of November Caras y Caretas gives his arrival two pages: the emir on the deck of the Chili, the crowd, the speakers, and the project he has announced to the press, to turn his colony toward agriculture and so answer the Senate session of the twelfth of September, where Manuel Láinez had called the Syro-Ottomans peddlers and no use. Days later he calls on Senator Joaquín V. González, who had answered first. He brings a translator, and finds him useless: both men have fluent French.
suggested_refs: Caras y Caretas no. 631, Buenos Aires, 5 November 1910, pp. 80-81, on the new Ottoman consul general

stops.name: Buenos Aires, essays for the Revista Argentina de Ciencias Políticas
stops.campa: Between consular duties Arslan turns scholar of his own vanishing world, publishing in Rodolfo Rivarola's Revista Argentina de Ciencias Políticas a run of essays no other man in Buenos Aires is positioned to write: La joven Turquía y Europa in 1911, La Tripolitania in the same year Italy seizes the last Ottoman province in Africa, and in 1913 a Historia diplomática de la Europa Balcánica tracing the wars then dismembering the Balkans. He writes as an insider watching his own empire's slow amputation from a lecture hall eight thousand miles from Constantinople, in a language he began learning at forty-two.
suggested_refs: Revista Argentina de Ciencias Políticas (ed. Rodolfo Rivarola), vols. II, III and VI, 1911-1913

stops.name: Estancia La Larga, a novel begun in Roca's country
stops.campa: General Julio Argentino Roca, twice president and the country's great pacifier of the pampas, invites the consul out to his estancia La Larga, on the Daireaux plain, expressly so that he can finish a book without distraction. Arslan says so himself in the dedication. The book is Final de un idilio, a novel of Riette of Alsace and the officer Van Doren, of Belgium invaded and Albert I standing; the country where Arslan had spent ten years of his life, burning. Part of it is written here before October 1914. Roca dies that October; the novel appears in 1917, dedicated to him.
suggested_refs: Estancia La Larga, partido de Daireaux, province of Buenos Aires
Final de un idilio (1917), dedicated to the memory of Julio A. Roca

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the friendship of the founder of La Plata
stops.campa: The bond with Joaquín V. González deepens past a single visit of thanks into a genuine friendship between two men of letters who happen also to hold office: González, former governor of La Rioja, founding president of the National University of La Plata, defender of immigrants in the Senate; Arslan, emir turned consul turned essayist, defender of his own colectividad in the press. Their correspondence and company will run a decade, ending only with González's death in December 1923, by which time Arslan has long since ceased to be anyone's consul and become instead an Argentine editor in his own right.
suggested_refs: Joaquín V. González, founder of the Universidad Nacional de La Plata
Emín Arslán, 'Joaquín V. González, íntimo', Revista Nosotros XLVI, 177 (1924): 201
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'El primer cónsul turco-otomano en la Argentina. La amistad de Emín Arslán y Joaquín V. González', Todo es Historia 572 (March 2015): 6-19

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the empire enters the war Arslan will not serve
stops.campa: The Ottoman Empire enters the World War at Germany's side at the end of October 1914, and in Buenos Aires the emir consul who spent a quarter century opposing the Sultan's despotism now finds his own government allied to the power he considers Europe's worst. He sends a memorandum to the Grand Vizier saying so, and its arithmetic is bleak and symmetrical: there is no outcome of this war in which his people are not the losers. Within days his usefulness to Constantinople, and Constantinople's patience with him, are both at an end. The bargain of 1897, dissent worn as a uniform, finally comes apart.
stops.quote: tanto si triunfaba Alemania como si era derrotada, nosotros seríamos los derrotados
stops.quote_source: Emín Arslán, recalling his 1914 memorandum to the Grand Vizier, in his 1921 letter published in Maǧallat Sarkīs, Cairo
suggested_refs: The Ottoman Empire's entry into the First World War, October-November 1914

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Argentine courts rule for the German consul
stops.campa: Rodolfo Bobrik, the German consul general who now represents Ottoman interests in Argentina by arrangement between the allied empires, demands that Arslan hand over the consulate's papers and seal. Arslan refuses without a direct order from the Grand Vizier himself, an old consul's punctilio turned into a last act of resistance; the dispute goes to the Argentine Supreme Court, which rules for Bobrik. Arslan surrenders the archive he no longer has any government to answer to, and with it the last formal thread tying him to the empire whose flag he once flew over the Río de la Plata.
suggested_refs: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación, Fallos 122:129 (1915), 'Bobrik, Rodolfo, cónsul general de Alemania c/ Arslan, Emir Emin, cónsul general de Turquía'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, 'Reflexiones de un condenado a muerte'
stops.campa: In the forty-fourth number of his own weekly, La Nota, Arslan publishes a column titled Reflexiones de un condenado a muerte. A Constantinople paper has carried the sentence. He had been given ten days to present himself to a court martial, a period in which no man could have crossed from Buenos Aires to Istanbul in that year; failing to appear, he was declared firari, a fugitive, condemned to death, his property confiscated. Since 1897 he has taken care to hold posts beyond the Porte's reach; the notice proves the precaution sound. He writes of it with irony, and no intention of going back to be hanged.
suggested_refs: La Nota, no. 44, Buenos Aires, 10 June 1916, 'Reflexiones de un condenado a muerte', pp. 862-863

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the desagravio at the cantina Ferrari
stops.campa: The same number carries the answer. His colleagues from the newsroom have taken the condemned man to dinner at the cantina of one Ivo Ferrari, whose name falls on the ear almost exactly as firari does, the fugitive word Constantinople hung on him; the whole joke of the desagravio is in that near-rhyme. Ramón Columba, the sharpest political caricaturist in the country, draws the emir's head brought in on a platter to the German Emperor, dressed for the occasion as Salome. It is the moment Buenos Aires decides, informally and years before any certificate, that the emir is one of theirs.
suggested_refs: 'Una condena festejada con un banquete' and Ramón Columba's caricature 'Salomé', La Nota no. 44, 10 June 1916
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

segments.name: La Nota and the War of Words (1915-1921)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first number of La Nota
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of August the first issue of La Nota appears from an office at 25 de Mayo 294, a weekly literary and political review founded and directed by the emir without a consulate, promising a tribune open to all the intellectuals of the River Plate. It keeps the promise: Lugones, Ingenieros, Ricardo Rojas, Rodó, Rubén Darío, Joaquín V. González, Alfredo Palacios, Gerchunoff, and in time a very young Alfonsina Storni, beside Arslan's own Oriental chronicles. It will run three hundred and twelve numbers, an important vehicle of Argentine letters made by a Druze emir who had learned Spanish, his fourth language, only five years before, at forty-two.
suggested_refs: La Nota, no. 1, Buenos Aires, 14 August 1915; offices at calle 25 de Mayo 294

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Nota carries the first word of the Armenian extermination
stops.campa: Within days of founding his review Arslan uses it to do what he did twenty years before in La Revue Blanche: carry news of a massacre past the borders that would suppress it. La Nota is among the first papers in Argentina to bring a general public word of the deportations and killings then under way against the empire's Armenian subjects. It is not a neutral consul's silence. It is the same man who wrote of 1896 from Paris exile, writing now of a second and far larger catastrophe, and who will end by weighing the two hands that did it and finding, appallingly, for the older one.
stops.quote: Si él asesinó a cien mil armenios, Enver ha hecho asesinar a un millón, exterminando casi toda una raza y la mitad de la Siria.
stops.quote_source: Emín Arslán, Recuerdos de Oriente (Buenos Aires, 1918), p. 216, comparing Abdülhamid II with Enver Pasha
suggested_refs: La Nota, August 1915, early reports of the Armenian deportations and massacres

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Unamuno reads La Nota from afar
stops.campa: Writing to Pedro Jiménez Ilundain on the twentieth of February, Miguel de Unamuno lets slip where his war writing is going: to Argentina, to La Nación, and to a weekly he assumes his correspondent has never heard of. In another letter, to Joaquín Montaner, he gives the emir's review its character in five words and sends Montaner the street address to submit to, naming the director: El Emir Emín Arslán. It is an interesting magazine, Unamuno says, and frankly Germanophobe. Within six months of its founding, La Nota is a channel through which one of the great voices of Spanish speaks to South America about the war.
stops.quote: Leo bastante y escribo algo, casi todo sobre la guerra, especialmente para la Argentina, en La Nación y en La Nota (¿conoce usted este semanario?)
stops.quote_source: Miguel de Unamuno, letter to Pedro Jiménez Ilundain, 20 February 1916
suggested_refs: Miguel de Unamuno, letter to Pedro Jiménez Ilundain, 20 February 1916
Epistolario Unamuno-Joaquín Montaner: 'una revista interesante, y francamente germanófoba'
sources: Unamuno, Epistolario americano 1890-1936 (ed. Laureano Robles, Salamanca 1996): 430
Tarín-Iglesias & Robles, 'Epistolario Miguel de Unamuno-Joaquín Montaner', Cuad. Cát. M. de Unamuno 35: 286

stops.name: Buenos Aires, 'La verdad sobre el harem'
stops.campa: The emir publishes La verdad sobre el harem, the truth about the harem, and with it takes up the peculiar office he will hold for the rest of his life: correcting his adopted country's fantasies about the world he came from. Buenos Aires in 1916 knows the Orient through French novels and operetta, all sherbet and captive women; Arslan, who grew up inside the society being romanced, dismantles the picture in the romancers' own language. It is the first of the books that make him, to Argentine readers, less a foreign consul than their resident authority on everything east of Trieste.
suggested_refs: Emin Arslan, La verdad sobre el harem (Buenos Aires, 1916)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Alfonsina Storni joins the pages of La Nota
stops.campa: Alfonsina Storni has been publishing early poems and prose in La Nota since 1916; from the twenty-eighth of March to the twenty-first of November of this year she is a permanent contributor, thirty-five pieces in all, among them Convalecer and Golondrinas. She is not yet the voice the continent will know. Arslan by now directs a magazine that has outgrown its founder's original purpose of self-defense and become simply part of the furniture of Buenos Aires literary life, indistinguishable from any native-born editor's review, though its director still signs himself, in the Arabic press across town, al-Amir Amin Arslan.
suggested_refs: La Nota, 28 March - 21 November 1919, Alfonsina Storni's contributions

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Nota closes after 312 numbers
stops.campa: Arslan directs La Nota in person to the twenty-ninth of October 1920 and its two hundred and seventy-second number, then hands the direction to Carlos Alberto Leumann, who had been his chief of the newsroom since 1916; the review runs to a final three hundred and twelve issues before closing in 1921, the same year the emir takes Argentine citizenship. Six years of a weekly begun as an exile's platform end as one more closed chapter of the country's periodical history, remembered less for its founder's politics than for the young writers, Storni foremost among them, whom it helped launch.
suggested_refs: La Nota, no. 272, 29 October 1920, Arslán's last number as director; Leumann's succession

stops.name: Punta del Este, La Chaumière on the Manzana 26
stops.campa: On the peninsula of Punta del Este, where he has summered since soon after his 1910 arrival, Arslan commissions the French architect Eduardo Le Monnier to build him a single-storey house of stone under a thatched roof, La Chaumière, on lots b, c, d and e of the resort's Manzana 26, the block the streets Muergos, Los Arrecifes and Resalsero close against the Rambla. The beach where he swims and receives his friends will come, in time, to carry his own title as its name: Playa El Emir. It is the one corner of the New World the Old World's last consul without an empire has made entirely his own.
suggested_refs: La Chaumière, Eduardo Le Monnier's 1920 cottage for Arslan at Punta del Este
Playa El Emir, Punta del Este, named for Arslan

stops.name: Buenos Aires, naturalization: 'a citizen of a respected state'
stops.campa: With the Ottoman Empire dissolved and its Arab provinces parceled into French and British mandates, Arslan formalizes what has been true in practice since 1914 and becomes an Argentine citizen. He explains the choice afterward in terms that are neither sentimental nor merely legal: whichever side had won the war, he says, the Arabs would have been the defeated, subordinated either to German ambition or to colonial partition. Better, then, to belong outright to a republic that owes him nothing and asks nothing of him but loyalty freely given.
stops.quote: Y que yo antes que ser súbdito de una colonia prefería ser ciudadano de un Estado respetado, especialmente si estaba dotado de una posición tan ilustre como el estado argentino.
stops.quote_source: Emín Arslán, letter to the director of La Razón explaining his naturalization, published in Arabic by Salīm Sarkīs in Maǧallat Sarkīs 24, Cairo, 15 December 1921: 765-768
suggested_refs: Arslan's Argentine naturalization, 1921
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a character in Lugones' Cuentos fatales
stops.campa: Leopoldo Lugones, the most commanding figure in Argentine letters and a contributor to La Nota, publishes Cuentos fatales, and in the tale El puñal he pronounces a secret word of the Druzes and so calls up, unmeaning it, a phantom visitor. The visitor speaks the emir's name, expounds certain hermetic Druze beliefs, and asks Lugones to intercede with Arslan on behalf of a mysterious Druze lady who must be persuaded home to Lebanon. Arslan does not object to being conjured; he uses the exotic curiosity as a magnet. In 1927 he will repay Lugones with Arabic lessons for his etymological dictionary.
suggested_refs: Leopoldo Lugones, Cuentos fatales (1924), 'El puñal'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Lápiz Azul, a satirical weekly
stops.campa: Arslan launches a new weekly, El Lápiz Azul, The Blue Pencil, humorous, political and literary, lighter in tone than La Nota had been, with the teacher and writer Celso Tíndaro, in life Pedro B. Franco, as secretary of the redaction, and contributions again from Lugones, from the composer Alberto Williams, from Eduardo Acevedo Díaz, and from the Spanish essayist Eugenio d'Ors. It runs forty-seven numbers to May of the following year, one more short-lived magazine in a career defined less by any single publication than by the sheer persistence of the habit: an emir without a country making, again and again, a small country out of print and paper.
suggested_refs: El Lápiz Azul, Buenos Aires, May 1925 - May 1926, 47 issues

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Asociación de Beneficencia Drusa
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of April Arslan founds the Sociedad Drusa de Beneficencia of Buenos Aires, a mutual-aid institution for a community smaller and less visible than the wider Syrian-Lebanese colectividad he has championed since 1910, gathering the scattered Druze families of Argentina, farmers and shopkeepers out of the same Lebanese mountain villages his own family once ruled as emirs, into a single benevolent association. It survives him by generations, and keeps at its house, to this day, books that were the founder's own: the three tongues of his three worlds shelved together at last.
suggested_refs: The Sociedad Drusa de Beneficencia, today the Asociación de Beneficencia Drusa, Buenos Aires, founded 26 April 1926

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Al-Istiklal and the cause of Syrian independence
stops.campa: As the Great Syrian Revolt burns against the French mandate in the homeland he left thirty-three years before, Arslan founds Al-Istiqlal, The Independence, printed wholly in Arabic though a part of its commercial notices run in Spanish, and in the same year publishes La revolución Siria contra el Mandato Francés. Both argue one case: that he backed the mandate in 1918 only on condition of total independence for Syria, and that what came instead is plain colonization in the vocabulary of trusteeship. Never, he writes, had they dreamed the Syrians' lot would be the Moroccans' or the Tunisians'. He will direct the paper to the day of his death.
stops.quote: no habrá paz entre el Oriente y el Occidente mientras Europa no se convenza de que ha llegado el término del dominio de una raza sobre otra
stops.quote_source: Emín Arslán quoting the orientalist Louis Massignon in 'Oriente contra Occidente', La Nación, Buenos Aires, 23 October 1927
suggested_refs: Al-Istiqlal / La Independencia, Buenos Aires, from June 1926 to 1943
Emin Arslan, La revolución Siria contra el Mandato Francés (Buenos Aires: Radio Cultura, 1926)
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Memorias written back into Arabic
stops.campa: At sixty-six the emir sits down to account for himself, and does it in Arabic. The Mudhakkarat come out in Buenos Aires from the Rustum brothers' press, at the author's own cost, under a title-page that gives his rank and then his ruin in one breath: by the pen of the emir Amin Arslan, formerly consul general of the Ottoman State. Everything is in them: Choueifat, the mudirate, Naum Pasha, Paris, the truce with a sultan he despised, Brussels, the revolution, the ocean. He writes them in the language of the mountain he left in 1893, for readers who mostly no longer have the country he is describing.
suggested_refs: Emín Arslán, Mudhakkarat (Memorias), Buenos Aires: Rustum Hermanos, 1934, author's edition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Misterios de Oriente
stops.campa: Misterios de Oriente gathers eight essays Arslan had first run in La Nota, one more volume in a long shelf, some Spanish, some Arabic, by which he has spent two decades explaining his birthplace to his adopted country: harems demystified, legends retold, history popularized for readers who would otherwise never know the mountain village of Choueifat existed. The exotic title is a lure and he knows it; behind it he tells the story of a people twice betrayed, by the sultan and by the mandate. Three editions will follow. Argentine literary Orientalism, such as it is, runs substantially through this one emir's pen.
suggested_refs: Emín Arslán, Misterios de Oriente; a Buenos Aires edition by Ed. Tor is recorded as 1932, es.wikipedia gives 1935
sources: Axel Gasquet, 'Historia, leyendas y clichés del Oriente en la obra de Emir Emin Arslán', CILHA 16 (2012)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the true history of 'Las Desencantadas'
stops.campa: Arslan publishes La verdadera historia de 'Las Desencantadas', correcting or completing, from his own vantage as an Ottoman insider turned Argentine writer, a story that had already passed into Western legend, the Turkish women said to have fled a sultan's harem for the freedom of the Bosphorus straits. It is exactly the work only Arslan can write: a man born inside the institution the West romanticizes, now explaining it in the West's own language, to the West's own reading public, seventy years after leaving the mountain that first taught him both tongues.
suggested_refs: Emín Arslán, La verdadera historia de 'Las Desencantadas' (Buenos Aires: Librería La Facultad, 1935)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Los Árabes: a lifetime's summa
stops.campa: In the same year he presides in Buenos Aires over the First Arab Congress, an independence conference gathering delegates of the Arab emigration to both Americas, Arslan at seventy-three publishes Los Árabes: reseña histórico-literaria y leyendas. It is the summa of everything thirty years of Argentine journalism had taught in fragments, and it argues its case defensively, calling European orientalists to the stand, Massignon, Le Bon, Asín Palacios, García Gómez, against the stereotypes he has spent a lifetime unpicking. It is his last book. Four editions will follow. It reads like a man closing an account honestly, leaving nothing owed.
suggested_refs: Emín Arslán, Los Árabes: reseña histórico-literaria y leyendas (Buenos Aires: Sopena, 1941)
The First Arab Congress, Buenos Aires, 1941, presided by Arslán

stops.name: Chacarita Cemetery, Buenos Aires: the emir's grave
stops.campa: Emin Arslan dies in Buenos Aires on the ninth of January, seventy-four years old, never married, without children, the last emir of his line to have governed any part of the Gharb and the first Muslim-born writer of the River Plate press to have been read for thirty years by Lugones, Storni, Ingenieros, and the whole literate republic he adopted. Next morning La Prensa and La Nación both carry his photograph. He is laid in a mausoleum at Chacarita, the great secular cemetery of the city that gave him citizenship in 1921 after his own empire disowned him. Al-Istiqlal, which he had directed to that last day, ceases with him.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of Emír Emín Arslán, Cementerio de la Chacarita, Buenos Aires
La Prensa (p. 7) and La Nación (p. 5), Buenos Aires, 10 January 1943
sources: Pablo Tornielli, 'Hombre de tres mundos', Dirasat Hispanicas 2 (2015): 157-181
